articles.title: Quote of the day by Michael Jordan: "You must expect great things of yourself before…" - a powerful reminder that great achievements begin with self-belief
articles.summary: US News: Michael Jordan's words speak to something a lot of people quietly wrestle with long before they ever attempt anything difficult, the question of wheth.
articles.body: Michael Jordan's words speak to something a lot of people quietly wrestle with long before they ever attempt anything difficult, the question of whether they genuinely believe they are capable of achieving it in the first place. "You must expect great things of yourself before you can do them," he said, a line that has been repeated so consistently over the years, across dozens of independent collections of his quotes, that it has become one of his most widely recognised statements on ambition and self-belief. The quote does not claim that simply expecting success guarantees it. Nobody, not even someone as accomplished as Jordan, gets to skip the actual work involved. What the quote highlights instead is how our own expectations quietly shape the effort, discipline and persistence we are actually willing to bring to a goal, often long before that goal has even properly taken shape.Quote of the day by Michael Jordan"You must expect great things of yourself before you can do them"What is the meaning of Michael Jordan's quoteThe quote suggests that your mindset genuinely shapes the way you approach your own goals, sometimes without you even fully noticing it happening. If you constantly assume that something is beyond your ability, you may hesitate to attempt it at all, or give up the moment the first obstacle appears in front of you. That instinct is entirely human. Nobody enjoys putting real effort into something they secretly suspect is doomed from the start. But when you genuinely expect yourself to improve and achieve more, something shifts. You are considerably more likely to challenge yourself, to put in the kind of sustained effort that actually produces results over time, and to keep working even when progress feels frustratingly slow. The expectation, in a very real sense, comes before the achievement ever does.Why self-belief genuinely mattersSelf-belief does not mean walking around convinced you are guaranteed to win at everything you try. That would be a fairly brittle kind of confidence, one that shatters the moment reality disagrees with it. Real self-belief means something quieter, believing that you are genuinely capable of learning, of improving, and of giving yourself an honest chance to succeed rather than assuming failure before you have even started. That distinction genuinely matters. Someone who believes they can become better is considerably more likely to actually practise after making a mistake, rather than deciding the mistake proves they were never any good in the first place. They are also more likely to accept honest criticism without becoming defensive, and to keep working towards a genuinely difficult objective long after the initial excitement of starting has worn off.Great achievements often begin with high expectationsMajor accomplishments rarely happen entirely by accident. Before someone becomes genuinely skilled at something, they generally have to believe, at least a little, that improvement is actually possible for them specifically. An athlete expects to become faster, even before their times have improved. A student expects to eventually understand a subject that currently feels completely impenetrable. An entrepreneur expects to build something genuinely valuable, long before there is any real evidence the business will work. Those expectations, however modest or bold, tend to create exactly the motivation needed to take the first genuine step, which is very often the hardest part of the whole process.Expecting more does not mean demanding perfectionThere is an important difference worth drawing out here between holding high standards and demanding something close to perfection from yourself. Jordan's message can be understood as encouraging people to aim higher, not to expect flawlessness the moment they begin. Failure, honest mistakes and genuine setbacks are simply part of pursuing any difficult goal worth having, and pretending otherwise tends to make setbacks feel considerably worse than they actually need to. A person can hold ambitious expectations for themselves while also genuinely accepting that real progress usually takes time, sometimes considerably longer than anyone would like.How expectations quietly influence effortWhat we expect from ourselves genuinely affects how much effort we are actually willing to invest in something. If a goal feels completely impossible from the outset, putting in extra effort can start to feel pointless, almost embarrassing, like trying too hard at something everyone secretly knows will not work out. But if we genuinely believe that improvement is achievable, even a genuinely difficult task can start to feel worth pursuing properly. That belief tends to encourage real consistency over time, which is very often considerably more important to eventual success than short, dramatic bursts of motivation that fade after a few days.Michael Jordan's career reflects the ideaJordan became one of basketball's most successful players in history, but his career was never built solely on natural talent alone. His reputation was shaped just as much by intense preparation, real competitiveness and a sustained willingness to keep improving even once he had already reached the top of his sport. His quote reflects a broader principle running through high performance generally, that before you can consistently perform at a genuinely high level, you first have to actually believe that reaching that level is possible for you specifically, not simply for other people who happen to look talented from the outside.Why low expectations can genuinely hold you backSometimes people quietly lower their own expectations as a kind of emotional protection against disappointment. If you expect very little from yourself, failure genuinely does hurt less when it arrives. That protection comes at a real cost though. Low expectations can also become genuinely limiting over time, discouraging people from attempting challenging opportunities altogether, or from ever properly discovering what they are actually capable of achieving when they genuinely try. Expecting more from yourself, even when it feels uncomfortable at first, tends to create a real willingness to take those chances anyway.Other memorable quotes by Michael Jordan"Everybody has talent, but ability takes hard work.""To learn to succeed, you must first learn to fail.""I can accept failure, everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying.""Some people want it to happen, some wish it would happen, and others make it happen."How to apply Michael Jordan's quote in everyday lifeSet ambitious goals, giving yourself something genuinely meaningful to actually work towards, rather than something so small it never really stretches you.Believe improvement is possible, since your current ability does not have to determine your future ability, however things look right now.Raise your standards gradually, aiming to become genuinely better rather than chasing an impossible idea of perfect.Take on difficult opportunities, since real growth very often begins just outside your comfort zone rather than safely within it.Keep practising consistently, since expectations only really become meaningful once they are followed by genuine, repeated effort.Learn honestly from failure, remembering that a setback does not have to change your belief in your own long-term potential.Avoid comparing yourself constantly to other people, and instead measure your progress against your own previous performance.Be patient with yourself, since genuinely high achievement usually takes repeated effort sustained over a considerably longer time than anyone expects.Challenge your own self-doubt directly, questioning the assumptions that quietly tell you something is automatically beyond your reach.Turn belief into real action, since expecting more from yourself only actually matters once it changes what you are genuinely willing to do.Why Michael Jordan's quote remains relevantIt is remarkably easy to underestimate yourself before you have even properly started. You may quietly decide that a goal is too difficult, that someone else is simply more talented, or that you are not genuinely capable of reaching a particular level. Jordan's quote offers a considerably different approach to all of that. Set the expectation first, and then work steadily towards actually becoming the person capable of meeting it. Great achievements rarely begin with total certainty that success is coming. They very often begin instead with something quieter and considerably more honest, the simple belief that you are capable of trying for something genuinely greater than whatever you have managed to achieve so far.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Police operation takes unexpected turn when officers stumble upon ancient burial cave
articles.summary: During a law enforcement operation tied to a violent family conflict, Israel Police discovered a Second Temple period burial cave beneath a building located in Silwan.
articles.body: Israeli police recently stumbled on an ancient burial cave in an unlikely place while carrying out an operation in Jerusalem. The discovery was announced by the Israel Police, Israel's civilian law enforcement agency, on Aug. 24. While carrying out an operation related to what police described as a "violent family conflict" in Silwan, a village in East Jerusalem, officers came upon the cave. ARCHAEOLOGISTS MAKE UNUSUAL FIND NEAR SITE WHERE ARK OF THE COVENANT WAS ONCE KEPT The operation followed a deadly clash between feuding families that erupted into gunfire and Molotov cocktail attacks, according to The Jerusalem Post. The violence prompted police to launch an operation aimed at locating those involved in the conflict. "As part of the activity, Jerusalem Border Police officers conducted searches in Silwan and accompanied government authority representatives at a compound where individuals involved in the incident reside," police said in a translated statement. Officers then found the burial cave beneath a building — along with other "archaeological finds." ANCIENT GOLD RING UNEARTHED AT GRAVE CARRIES 2,000-YEAR-OLD SECRET MESSAGE "Representatives of the Israel Antiquities Authority arrived at the scene, and an initial examination indicates that the graves date to the Second Temple period," police said. "Security forces are securing the scene to allow for the continued handling and examination of the finds." Rock-cut burial caves were commonly used as family tombs in Jerusalem during the Second Temple period, though officials did not provide a more precise date for the newly discovered graves. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Second Temple period lasted from roughly 516 B.C. to 70 A.D., when Roman forces destroyed the temple during the First Jewish-Roman War. Pictures released by Israeli police show the dark interior of the rock-cut burial cave, with debris scattered across the floor. Fox News Digital reached out to the Israel Police and the Israel Antiquities Authority for additional comment. articles.title: Missing tally rises to 2,482, including 320 Indians, as disaster toll hits 584
articles.summary: South Asia News: NEW DELHI: At least 584 people were dead and 2,482 missing across Nepal and Tibet by Friday evening after the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster, with Nepa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At least 584 people were dead and 2,482 missing across Nepal and Tibet by Friday evening after the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster, with Nepal accounting for 579 deaths and 1,924 missing and Tibet reporting five dead and 558 missing. The scale remained fluid, as Nepal Police maintained a higher list of those unaccounted for; tunnel searches continued and large numbers of people remained cut off or out of communication.Rescue teams on both sides of the border were repeatedly forced to reassess and retreat Friday as an unstable barrier lake overflowed into Bhote Koshi river, sent a fresh surge downstream and briefly halting operations. Hours later, another avalanche dumped an estimated 50,000 cubic metres of ice debris. Satellite images later showed an even more worrying development — a second, larger upstream lake was still growing and had no visible outlet.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said 320 Indian nationals in Nepal remained “uncontactable” on Friday, up from 290 earlier, while around 100 persons of Indian origin holding other nationalities were also out of contact. Jaiswal said it was a “dynamic situation”. India had not confirmed any deaths by Friday evening and MEA said it was seeking clarity from Nepalese authorities.MEA said at least 84 nationals had been rescued in Nepal — 63 workers from Trishuli-1 and 21 pilgrims from Tamil Nadu. The group of 21 reached Delhi on Friday. “First, good news: 21 Indian nationals who had yesterday arrived in Kathmandu from the area which was affected by the flood have landed in Delhi,” Jaiswal said.In addition, MEA said 149 Indians crossed into Nepal from Tibet on Friday and around 400 more were safe on the Chinese side.In Nepal, the official missing count nearly doubled within hours to close to 2,000 as authorities added fresh lists from devastated settlements, hydropower projects and tourism groups. The country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said 4,451 people had been rescued. India said 320 of its nationals in Nepal remained uncontactable.The rapidly changing figures reflected the enormous task of reconciling reports from families, district administrations, employers, tour operators and security agencies as rescuers reached previously inaccessible areas.Rescuers fight tough terrain to reach those trapped in tunnelsHydropower sites accounted for an extraordinary share of those unaccounted for. NDRRMA said 933 people linked to projects remained missing, while the ministry of energy said reports from promoters indicated that more than 1,000 workers had at one stage lost contact. “There are reports that more than a thousand people working on hydropower projects have lost contact,” ministry spokesperson Mohan Shakya said.The largest concentration was at the Korean-funded 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 project, where workers had taken shelter inside tunnels as floodwater and debris destroyed access routes. Initial information indicated around 400 people were inside the tunnel and another 176 outside were uncontactable. Officials said about 40 Indians and eight Koreans working at the project were unaccounted for; around 100 Chinese workers had also been employed there, with some rescued.Project liaison officer Giri Adhikari said debris had entered the roughly 10km tunnel. “There should be no shortage of oxygen inside. There is a shortage of food and water. If rescued in time, it is estimated that those inside are still alive,” he said. With roads and tunnel approaches washed away, Adhikari said rescuers could reach some access points only by being lowered from helicopters along the cliff.Other hydropower projects also reported large numbers “out of contact”. Officials listed 93 at Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project alone.In Tibet’s Gyirong County, China reported five people dead and 558 missing, including 260 foreign nationals. Beijing had not released a nationality-wise breakdown of the missing foreigners as yet.Chinese authorities separately said they had moved all stranded tourists out of the accessible Gyirong area. A total of 555 tourists were evacuated, while 499 villagers and construction workers affected by the disaster were moved to shelters or other safe locations. Xinhua said no tourists remained stranded in the areas covered by that evacuation operation, although hundreds of people remain officially missing in the wider disaster zone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Millionaire’s £3m Bath mega-mansion sparks planning row as more than 100 residents demand seven-bedroom home be torn down; locals claim it is taller and larger than council-approved plans
articles.summary: UK News: A £3 million mega-mansion under construction on the outskirts of Bath has sparked a bitter planning dispute, with more than 100 local residents object.
articles.body: A £3 million mega-mansion under construction on the outskirts of Bath has sparked a bitter planning dispute, with more than 100 local residents objecting to the property and some calling for it to be demolished.According to a report by The Daily Mail, residents claim the huge seven-bedroom home on Bailbrook Lane is significantly taller and has a larger footprint than the property originally approved by Bath and North East Somerset Council.With construction nearing completion, the developer has submitted a retrospective planning application seeking approval for changes made during the build.The dispute has raised concerns among residents over whether the planning system is being exploited by wealthy developers who make substantial changes after receiving permission.Residents claim mega-mansion is much larger than approvedThe property is believed to be one of the largest new-build homes constructed in Bath in around a century.Neighbour Tavis Hamilton, 48, who lives with his partner Charlotte Bolton and their daughter, estimated the completed property could be worth around £3 million."It is enormous and dwarfs all the cottages," Hamilton said, claiming around 24 of the neighbouring cottages could fit within its footprint.He said the development had been under construction for around three years but that its full height and scale had only recently become clear as the building reached the final stages.Hamilton claims the original planning permission was for a low-lying, single-storey property designed to sit within the hillside alongside a lane lined with traditional Georgian buildings.However, he said construction workers encountered groundwater while excavating the site and subsequently filled part of the excavation with concrete.According to enforcement investigations, several aspects of the development differ from the approved plans, including its height, footprint and location on the site.Seven bedrooms instead of fiveResidents have also raised concerns about changes to the property's size and layout.The original proposal was for a five-bedroom house, while the latest plans show a seven-bedroom property.One resident wrote in an objection submitted through the council's planning website that the property had already been described as the largest house approved by the council for the site.They argued that increasing it to seven bedrooms made it even more out of keeping with Bailbrook Lane, which includes a historic listed church.Residents have also claimed that the property's orientation, siting, height, volume, footprint and landscaping differ substantially from the original plans.Hamilton described the development as "hugely overbearing" and said it had changed the character of the lane and affected views of the listed church.Some residents have even called for the property to be demolished, although Hamilton acknowledged that such action would be an extreme measure.Developer denies trying to bypass planning rulesThomas Worrall, a director of TKB Property Developments and TK Building Company Ltd and the applicant named in the latest planning documents, has rejected accusations that he deliberately circumvented planning rules.Worrall said he purchased the site with planning permission already in place because he wanted to build a family home."The whole street has been against me from day one," he said, insisting that he was not trying to "play the system".According to Worrall, problems with the ground made it difficult to construct the property according to the original plans."There have been complications on the ground and the professional builders were not able to make it work, so it was a little bit higher to start with," he said.Worrall said he has now stopped construction while the planning application is considered."I've now pulled all my guys off site and am trying to deal with the planners," he said.Developer says changes were necessary because of groundwaterDocuments submitted with the retrospective application state that the changes were made because some elements of the original design could not be practically or safely constructed.The applicant said groundwater was "constant" at the lower basement level, leaving the ground saturated."The only way that could be stabilised was to stop where they did and fill it with hardcore," the documents state. The material was then used to create a stable base for the concrete foundation.The applicant also said engineering work revealed that some elements of the original proposal would not work in practice.Changes included additional basement areas, alterations to the roof, modifications to windows and changes to the access.The developer maintains that efforts were made to keep the building's height as low as possible."We have tried to keep the building as low as we could, and we feel that the overall height of the building is similar to the approved plans," the application documents state.The applicant also argued that the property's overall scale and appearance had "hardly changed from the initial approved plans."Worrall says he simply wants to move into the houseWorrall said the controversy has caused him significant stress and that he even attempted to sell the property around a year ago."I just want an easy life. I want to get my house finished and move my family into it," he said.He also said the construction problems had forced him to abandon plans for a swimming pool in the basement because workers could not excavate any deeper."It was causing so much stress about a year ago I tried to sell it. But it was a mess, and no one would buy it, so I had to tinker on," Worrall said.He added that he believed the finished property would eventually be a positive addition to the area."Once it's complete, it will be a lovely building," he said. "I am sorry to everyone for the inconvenience of it all. But I want to be a good neighbour."Councillor backs residents' enforcement demandsLocal ward councillor Joanna Wright has backed calls for enforcement action and described the situation as "outrageous"."They got planning permission in 2013, and they haven't built it to that plan. They keep extending it and changing who owns it," Wright said.She argued that the case demonstrated how wealthy developers could use their understanding of the planning system to keep pursuing changes."I understand the anger local residents feel about the whole process," she said. "They are told they cannot do things, and that is the end of it."Wright also pointed to the property's size and its proximity to a Grade II listed church, saying the development would be taller and larger than the neighbouring heritage building."It is one rule for a wealthy person - they get what they want by playing the system - and another for everyone else," she said.Council will consider enforcement after planning decisionMore than 70 residents attended a recent site meeting, while more than 100 objections have reportedly been submitted against the latest proposal.Residents have called for construction to remain halted while the extensive changes are assessed.Bath and North East Somerset Council declined to comment on the case, saying enforcement action would only be considered after the retrospective planning application has been determined.The application is currently being assessed.For now, the future of the controversial Bath mega-mansion remains in the hands of planners, with residents seeking enforcement action and the developer hoping the changes can ultimately be approved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
articles.summary: Kai Wegner says the German capital and city-state would not cave in to a ransom demand for data stolen in a cyber-attack.
articles.body:
Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said.

Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m).

Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken.

The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility.

It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters.

"Berlin will not be blackmailed," Wegner said on Friday.

He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity".

Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August.

Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days.

Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said.

"It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday.

Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details.

It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports.

The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries.

It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files.

When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web.

The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised.

articles.title: New York's Erie County axes DHS job fair over ICE's role, drawing backlash: 'Totally inappropriate'
articles.summary: Mark Poloncarz urged the Buffalo Convention Center to cancel a DHS career expo over ICE's participation, sparking a clash with Erie County legislators.
articles.body: A Buffalo-area Republican accused Democratic Erie County Executive Mark Poloncarz of overstepping his authority after the Buffalo Convention Center canceled a two-day Department of Homeland Security career expo set to begin Tuesday because officials objected to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's participation and warned of possible protests. "The county executive has completely surpassed his power and authority. This was totally inappropriate for him to call on the management of the convention center to cancel this event," Republican Erie County Legislator Lindsay Lorigo said in an interview with Fox News Digital. Lorigo said she understood discussions about the event were continuing and hoped the center would reverse its decision. She said vendors had invested time and local labor into the expo’s setup. DEMOCRATIC MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED' "I have had discussions with vendors that are already set up there," Lorigo said. "They’re concerned that they’re going to have to close down their business because they can’t afford the hundreds of thousands of dollars, but now they don’t know who’s going to pay the bill. "I think he is blowing the safety concern out of the water." DHS sharply defended ICE in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday and rejected criticism as political. "Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage. Where is the outrage for Angel families who lost a loved one to illegal alien crime?" a DHS spokesperson said. "To most Americans, our brave ICE law enforcement are heroes. Eighty percent of Americans support arresting and deporting criminal illegal aliens from American neighborhoods." AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION A May Harvard CAPS/Harris online survey found 80% supported deporting immigrants who are in the country illegally and committed crimes. USAJOBS described the expo as the department’s premier large-scale hiring event. It was open to the public, veterans, military spouses, people with disabilities and recent graduates, with recruiting planned across cybersecurity, intelligence, law enforcement, finance, human resources, immigration services, logistics and transportation security. New York Labor Department data released Tuesday showed 25,100 people were unemployed in the Buffalo-Cheektowaga area in July. Its 4.4% jobless rate was up from 4.3% a year earlier. DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE In a joint statement released by Poloncarz’s office Thursday, the county executive said Erie County owns the convention center but does not manage its bookings or daily operations. Poloncarz said he learned of the expo Wednesday and urged its management corporation to cancel the DHS contract. "The Buffalo Convention Center is a publicly owned community asset, and I do not believe it should be used to support recruitment efforts that are inconsistent with the values we have repeatedly expressed as a welcoming community," Poloncarz said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Convention center President and CEO Patrick Kaler said management first asked DHS to hold the event without ICE. "When it became clear that was not possible, we made the decision to cancel as we feel it’s in the best interests of our community at this time," Kaler said. articles.title: Richard Gadd's Edinburgh: 'Arrive with an idea, leave with a career'
articles.summary: The Baby Reindeer star says the festivals are essential for new talent, and that he owes his success to the Fringe.
articles.body:
Richard Gadd says he owes everything to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe.

His show Baby Reindeer, a dark comedy about his experience of a stalker, won a string of awards, and enjoyed a sell-out run in Edinburgh before transferring to the London stage.

But it was the arrival of executives from the TV Festival in the final week of August in 2019, which took his career on a whole new trajectory.

"The show had sold out before the festival had even begun," he told a gathering at a Screen Scotland event to launch a new TV festival.

"This was exactly 10 years after my debut at the Fringe where I had to cancel a show because nobody had turned up.

"It was the talk of the festival, and at the end of the month, I got a message from my manager to say Netflix wanted me but so did the BBC and HBO and Channel 4."

He eventually made the TV show for Netflix, where it became a cultural phenomenon, topping their streaming platforms globally.

It went on to win a stream of awards, including six Emmys, before Gadd moved onto his next project, Half Man, with the BBC, which was screened earlier this year.

Gadd, who grew up in Wormit in Fife, first connected with the Fringe through the National Theatre of Scotland show Black Watch, which premiered at the 2006 festival before touring nationally and internationally.

"It was a brutally funny ensemble piece, part-dance epic about the Iraq war, the camaraderie of soldiers, and the desperation of lost youth," he said.

"And as the lights went down on the final seconds of the show, I remember the entire audience getting to their feet with tears in their eyes and I knew that I had witnessed history.

"I remember watching the lights of Edinburgh disappearing out the window and thinking THIS is what I want to do. "

Four years later, he made his own Fringe debut at the Argyle Cellar Bar.

"I'm wearing a thong and I'm head to toe in baby oil having just danced to Tom Jones' sex bomb, and there's an embarrassed couple in the front row still clapping me in an otherwise empty room.

"I ask them for donations at the end of the show and they end up giving me two pounds. It was 2009. I'm 20 years old and I've just started doing comedy.

"I've flyered all day and all night, but despite my best efforts, I've performed to audiences of no more than five people."

He added: "Sometimes, indeed most times, I had to cancel the show because nobody turned up. Once, my audience was so small, I ended up taking them for a drink instead.

"His name was Douglas, and he admitted coming to my show because the sight of me flyering outside his office for two weeks had been too much to bear."

The fringe's tradition of using every space as a stage found him performing in some unlikely places.

"One venue didn't have a door. Not even a curtain. Halfway through the show, people would wander through looking for the bathroom.

He says the festival gave him the chance to experiment in a way the comedy circuit never did. And the result was his first four-star review.

In 2014, he performed a show called Breaking Gadd – which he said disappointed scores of fans of that other hit TV show.

"They came, expecting anecdotes about Walter White and instead got a man in a jockstrap talking about all the ways he wanted to kill his family," he recalled.

During a later show, his routine involved biting into a bar of soap.

"I took a bite, and immediately the most excruciating burning sensation fills my mouth. My eyes were instantly popping, and my mouth filled with ulcers by the second.

"I snatched a pint from a random spectator's hand to wash it out with, but the burning sensation was between my teeth.

"In the end, we pulled the show early, and I find myself in A&E.

"When the doctor asked me what I'd done, I said, I ate a bar of soap. They looked at me for what felt like an eternity before asking 'Edinburgh Festival?'"

Gadd's 2015 show Waiting for Gadot brought further acclaim and he called the bar where he worked in Camden to tell them he wasn't coming back.

"Craig, my manager asked what I was going to do instead. I told him, I'm going to be a comedian and I hung up the phone."

In 2016, he performed Monkey See Monkey Do, which won him the Edinburgh Comedy award.

Although the performance was surreal with Gadd running on a treadmill throughout while being chased by a gorilla on the screen behind, the content detailed his experience of sexual abuse.

The show sold out, won rave reviews and brought acceptance from friends and family of the trauma he had not previously shared.

"My fears of judgement vanished in an instant," he said. "The weight of trauma lifted night after night. Is this what happens when you reveal your darkest secrets to the world?

"I found the most phenomenal freedom, and realised what it was all about.

"I remember when I went out to collect the Edinburgh comedy award that month, Something I'd dreamed about from the moment I first learned of its existence.

"I said, the worst thing my abuser ever did was take my confidence away, and I suppose this goes some way to getting it back."

As well as Baby Reindeer, the fringe has been the launch pad for Fleabag, Taskmaster, Six the Musical, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, Stomp, Flight of the Conchords, Garth Merengue, Alan Partridge, Mr Bean, The League of Gentlemen, Jerry Springer the Opera, Operation Mincemeat, and The Mighty Boosh.

Gadd hopes the launch of a new TV festival to replace the industry event which is moving to Manchester in 2027, will be vital to the festivals as they prepare to mark their 80th anniversary.

But he says he's concerned about spiralling costs, especially when it comes to accommodation.

"The fringe is nothing without giving new voices a chance to experiment, to take breaks, to hitch their car to a crazy idea and see what comes of it, to fail spectacularly but come back the next night to try again," he said.

"The festival risks becoming something that only those with enough money can afford to do. And that's what worries me."

He said if the Fringe became too expensive, too commercial, and too difficult to access, it could mean losing the very thing that makes it extraordinary.

"We could lose why it started in the first place," he added. "We could lose the place where someone could arrive with an idea and leave with a career."

articles.title: Tennessee governor plans to name Nashville airport after Dolly Parton
articles.summary: Thousands of fans have signed an online petition asking the airport to be named after her.
articles.body:
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has announced plans to name Nashville International Airport after Dolly Parton, following the 80-year-old country star's death from cancer this week.

The news comes after legions of fans signed an online petition to rename the airport after Parton, who was born in rural Tennessee and later moved to Nashville.

In a statement, Lee said he had spoken to Parton's team, who "expressed their appreciation for the extraordinary outpouring of support to honor Dolly".

"Dolly Parton's extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state," Lee said.

"At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state's favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly's music, generosity, faith, and kindness," the governor's statement said on Friday.

The online petition to rename the airport was originally launched in January 2025, but gained fresh momentum following her death and had gathered nearly 160,000 signatures by Friday evening.

"What a wonderful way to share her light and magic across Tennessee and the world," the petition says of the move to name the airport after Parton.

How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading

The BBC has asked the Dolly Parton Foundation for comment.

The name would need support from the Metro Nashville Airport Authority board, which is holding a meeting on the issue on 17 September, the governor's office said.

The final decision would require approval from the Federal Aviation Administration.

A lawmaker also pledged in recent days to introduce legislation in the statehouse to rename the airport in Parton's honour.

The US has named several airports after famous musicians and other celebrities, including Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky.

Parton won 10 Grammy awards and sold 100 million records worldwide, including hits like Coat of Many Colors, 9 to 5, Jolene, and I Will Always Love You.

articles.title: Thousands take part in March on Washington to promote voting rights
articles.summary: Protest draws crowds to Washington, DC amid Trump’s threats of interference, voting restrictions in midterm elections.
articles.body:
Thousands of demonstrators have converged on the United States capital of Washington, DC, to warn of threats to voting rights ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Friday’s event marked the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington, an historic 1963 protest that galvanised the US civil rights movement.

But this year’s march had a theme that gestured to the midterms: “Defend the vote.” Civil rights leaders spoke of troubling trends that they feared would erode the voting power of Black and minority citizens.

“We know in this fight we’re fighting powerful forces, but this is why we rally today,” said Marc Morial, president and CEO of the National Urban League, a civil rights organisation.

“This is why we seek to bring Americans together of goodwill from all races, from all sections of the country, to push back as forcefully as we can.”

Since taking office for a second term, President Donald Trump has undertaken efforts to restrict voting that critics fear will limit access for lower-income and minority voters.

That includes advocating for greater proof of citizenship before voting. But those standards would require access to documents like birth certificates or passports that may not be accessible to everyone.

Speakers at the march also denounced a Supreme Court decision in April to strike down key provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 , a landmark piece of civil rights legislation.

The law was designed to crack down on practices that disenfranchised Black voters. For decades, it had prevented lawmakers from redrawing congressional districts based on race.

But in April’s ruling, the court’s conservative majority argued it was impossible to “disentangle race from politics”. It therefore declared that a congressional map could be struck down only when there was evidence that states had “intentionally” limited opportunities for non-white voters through “strong interference”.

Critics say that new legal standard effectively made discrimination on the basis of race legal for the purposes of drawing voting maps.

In the aftermath of the court’s ruling, a number of Republican-led states passed new congressional maps to favour their party, often by carving up majority-Black districts.

In a letter, Reverend Al Sharpton, an organiser of Friday’s march, drew a line between the fight for voting rights during the civil rights era and the present-day circumstances.

“We stand on the same ground because the work is not finished,” Sharpton said, referring to the site of the 1963 march. “The right to vote, the very foundation of our power, is being chipped away in statehouse after statehouse. When the vote is weakened, every other right grows fragile with it.”

Senator Bernie Sanders, a progressive leader, also told the crowd that the “dream of a more just and equitable society has never been under greater threat than it is right now”. He denounced Trump for his actions to weaken voting rights.

“Today, we have a president along with the Supreme Court members he appointed carrying out the most significant assault on voting rights since segregation, targeting virtually every aspect of the electoral system,” Sanders said.

articles.title: Hochul boasts 'I just banned it' as New York outlaws local police partnerships with ICE
articles.summary: Kathy Hochul says 287(g) agreements are now banned in New York, but DHS warns the restriction will force more federal agents into communities.
articles.body: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday on "Morning Joe" that New York banned formal civil immigration enforcement agreements between local law enforcement and ICE because she wants officers focused on local crime. A DHS spokesperson said in an exclusive statement to Fox News Digital that the restriction will force more federal agents into communities as 15 county sheriffs challenge the law in federal court. "When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have to have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities," the DHS spokesperson said. BORDER CZAR HOMAN VOWS TO 'FLOOD' NEW YORK WITH ICE AGENTS DESPITE HOCHUL'S RESISTANCE "Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. Instead of working with us, Governor Hochul and Attorney General James are choosing to RELEASE violent criminals from their jails directly back into our communities to perpetrate more crimes and create more victims." DHS cited five New York cases involving noncitizens who it said remained at large or were released despite ICE detainers after arrests or convictions involving attempted murder, rape, assault, weapons charges or child endangerment. ICE later took all five into custody, and one was removed to Mexico, the department said. Hochul’s office responded to DHS’s criticism Friday in a statement to Fox News Digital, disputing the department’s characterization of the law’s public safety consequences. "Governor Hochul has been clear: You don't make New York State safer by co-opting local law enforcement to conduct civil immigration enforcement that targets families, children and hardworking individuals," a Hochul spokesperson said. "A federal court has already upheld New York’s Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, and the state will continue to work with federal and local law enforcement in cracking down on violent offenders while keeping our communities safe and enforcing our laws." During the interview on "Morning Joe," co-host Willie Geist asked whether ICE could still secure agreements with New York police forces. DEM GOVERNOR IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER TESTING LIMITS OF AUTHORITY WITH MAJOR MOVE AGAINST ICE "I just banned it," Hochul said. "It's against the law now in the state of New York to have these agreements." The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, signed in May, took effect Tuesday. It prohibits state and local entities from entering or remaining in 287(g) agreements, which allow trained local personnel to perform certain federal civil immigration functions under ICE supervision. Hochul's office said the law does not prevent jails from notifying ICE about potentially deportable people in custody or transferring someone lawfully in custody to the agency, subject to local laws. Existing corrections law also requires the state Department of Corrections and Community Supervision to notify federal immigration authorities after receiving a noncitizen into custody, the governor's office said. NEW YORK SHERIFFS 'MAD AS HELL' AS HOCHUL PUSHES TO BAN KEY LAW ENFORCEMENT PARTNERSHIP The federal lawsuit, led by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault, claims the ban unlawfully overrides independently elected sheriffs’ authority and impairs federally authorized agreements. The state said Rensselaer was the only one of 12 agencies with a 287(g) agreement that had not indicated it would dissolve the pact. Attorney General Letitia James sued Rensselaer County and its sheriff Thursday, seeking an order terminating the agreement. The action was the first filed by the state’s new Office of Immigrant Trust. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A federal judge earlier this month denied the Justice Department’s request for a preliminary injunction against the 287(g) ban in a separate case, allowing Tuesday’s deadline to take effect. That litigation remains pending, and the 15 sheriffs have separately requested emergency relief in their new case.

articles.title: ‘Your small help means a lot’: Sacramento community rallies for Nepal flood victims
articles.summary: Hundreds of people are reported dead and thousands missing after a glacial collapse triggered destructive flooding near the Nepal-Tibet border, with the deva...
articles.body:
Hundreds of people are reported dead and thousands missing after a glacial collapse triggered destructive flooding near the Nepal-Tibet border, with the devastation being felt nearly 8,000 miles away in Sacramento's Nepali community.

Members of the Greater Sacramento Nepali Community Center say they struggled to contact loved ones in Nepal after the flooding disrupted electricity and phone service.

"They have no idea because there is no connection, no electricity, no telephone," Deepak Maskey, president of the Greater Sacramento Nepali Community Center, said. "They were just scared about what happened. looking for information about their families, friends and especially extended families."

Jagadish Shrestha, secretary of the Greater Sacramento Nepali Community Center, has relatives directly affected by the flooding.

"There are more and more devastating videos and pictures," Shrestha said. "We really feel bad and we've tried to contact our family in Nepal."

When Shrestha was eventually able to make contact, he learned one of his relatives had been trapped on a roof for more than a day.

"It's very bad. I feel very bad," Shrestha said. "But then I was like, feel lucky when I heard they rescued her."

Shrestha said his family is among many dealing with the aftermath of the disaster.

"The situation in Nepal [is] very miserable," Shrestha said. "A lot of people lost their life, and still, they are recovering a lot of bodies."

Following news of the flooding, the Greater Sacramento Nepali Community Center's board held emergency meetings to discuss how it could help people affected by the disaster.

"If something happens, how we can unite it? How can we help?" Maskey said. "Help, it shouldn't be big, it can be small. If you can contribute even a small part, that will make a huge difference when you are in need."

After those discussions, the community center said it plans to provide financial donations and is asking members of the Sacramento-area community to contribute.

"Everybody, please just help," Shrestha said. "Your small help, it means a lot. It's a really difficult time for Nepal. I wish all the people are going to recover soon from this difficult situation."

The Greater Sacramento Nepali Community Center is providing updates on its efforts through its Facebook page.

articles.title: Spain asks EU for help to process 5,000 Ceuta migrants amid local unrest
articles.summary: Thousands of migrants remain in the Spanish enclave, triggering anger among Ceuta residents.
articles.body:
Spain has asked Europe’s Border and Coastguard Agency, Frontex, for help to process some 5,000 migrants in Ceuta who crossed into the North African territory one month ago.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent the request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission’s director general for migration and home affairs, on Friday.

Grande-Marlaska also requested an extra 10 Frontex officers to speed up screening efforts.

Spanish authorities must identify those remaining in Ceuta to establish whether they are entitled to international protection or, if not, begin procedures for their return.

Authorities say between 5,000 and 8,000 migrants, including unaccompanied children, still in Ceuta are among the 72,000 people who crossed the border from Morocco on July 30.

The rush killed 82 people on the Spanish side of the border and 14 on the Moroccan side, according to official numbers. Human rights groups reported higher figures.

Spain’s request comes amid rising tensions in Ceuta, after a series of protests by residents who have demanded the migrants leave.

Tents on Trampolin Beach, where many migrants have been camping, have been attacked and set on fire.

Twelve migrants were arrested on Thursday after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and four migrants. Eleven were expelled from Ceuta, El Pais newspaper reported on Friday, citing sources from the city’s main court.

On Tuesday, Madrid made a formal request for emergency funding from the EU to help address the situation.

articles.title: Cambodia’s claim to have ended scam compounds met with scepticism
articles.summary: Cambodia’s claim of eradicating its scam compounds met with scepticism from Amnesty International and industry experts.
articles.body:
Cambodia says it no longer hosts any of the scam compounds that made the country a global hub for cybercrime, as rights groups and analysts cautioned that the claim cannot be independently verified.

According to a statement released on Friday, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the government’s ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, told 50 foreign diplomats and international officials on Thursday that “large-scale scam activities have been brought fully under control, and there are currently no online scam compounds remaining in the country”.

The statement said the achievement follows “the complete eradication of large-scale online scam operations, strict legal actions against perpetrators, networks and involved officials, alongside the systematic establishment of a cybersecurity legal framework”.

However, the statement acknowledged that criminal groups have shifted to decentralised operations – hiding in guesthouses, condominiums, rental houses, vehicles and coffee shops – which authorities said they will continue to target.

The compounds, largely run by Chinese criminal syndicates, have proliferated across Cambodia , Laos, the Philippines and Myanmar-Thai border areas since the pandemic. Reuters news agency said it has not independently confirmed the eradication claim.

Amnesty International’s co-regional director, Montse Ferrer, said the rights group is “highly skeptical of suggestions the scamming compound industry has been effectively eliminated”, adding: “The true test of long-term success is not how many compounds have closed, but whether the actors responsible have been investigated, prosecuted and prevented from resuming operations.”

Mark Taylor, an independent anti-trafficking consultant, said: “The strong confidence placed in the [Cambodian] government’s assertion that all scamming operations in Cambodia have been eradicated is severely misplaced.

“There are credible indicators that significant scamming operations continue and that recruitment of foreign workers into Cambodia for scamming work continues.”

Chhay Sinarith, the senior minister, said law enforcement investigated 793 suspected locations and raided 624 sites between July 2025 and August 20, 2026 , detaining nearly 30,000 suspects representing 39 nationalities.

Authorities rescued and deported 58,266 foreign nationals, while 3,477 suspects from 29 nationalities were arrested and jailed pending trial, he added.

articles.title: What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans
articles.summary: Households and businesses have become used to tariffs impacting the cost of living for more than year now, so what will change now?
articles.body:
A raft of new tariffs have been announced during the latest escalation of the trade war between the US and Canada.

The North American neighbours have been locked in a bitter economic conflict since US President Donald Trump launched his flagship trade policy on his return to the White House.

This week saw the latest move by the Canadians with Prime Minister Mark Carney imposing retaliatory import taxes on a host of US goods, after Trump threatened hikes of his own.

As the dust settles in this tit-for-tat tariff row, what will be affected most on both sides of the border?

If Trump's threat to raise tariffs on Canadian vehicles from 25% to 50% from 1 January 2027 becomes a reality, then that would deal a further blow to the automotive industry.

Cars, trucks and parts are among the main goods traded between the US, Canada and Mexico, with the manufacturing sector and supply chains stretching across borders.

Despite previous tariffs increasing costs for manufacturers, car dealerships have absorbed the "lion's share" to date, according to Bernard Yaros, lead economist at Oxford Economics.

"But that cushion is wearing thin," he adds. "The recently threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks, and car parts would feed through to consumer prices more readily than before."

Yaros thinks higher costs on imports to the US could accelerate a trend of manufacturers prioritising luxury cards, SUVs and pick-up trucks and push up prices in the used-car market if supplies of new but less-expensive vehicles becomes tight.

Carney has decided not to match Trump's 50% tariff threat so far, but a 25% import tax on certain American vehicles has been in place since last year.

Construction materials such as steel, aluminium as well as lumber wood have had tariffs in place before the latest escalation, though Canada has now matched US rates on the metals at 50%.

Carney has also imposed import taxes on several US wood products, such as plywood, and even screws used to fix timber together.

That means building firms that import such materials will face higher costs and may choose to pass those on through higher prices - pushing up the cost of homes, for example.

The Forest Products Association of Canada says tariffs would "raise costs on both sides of the border", while on the US side, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) urged Trump to make building materials exempt from his tariff agenda due to an "ongoing housing affordability crisis".

"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," he says.

In 2024 the US imported $23bn (C$32bn, £17bn) worth of wood products, with almost half from Canada, according to a US Congress report.

But the so-called "lumber wars" between the nations on soft wood used in housebuilding are not new and stretch back decades.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

A key factor in this episode of the tariff war is the volume of household items that have been specifically targeted as opposed to raw materials.

Carpets, washing machines, furniture, fridges and even knives, forks and spoons are set to have tariffs applied by Canada.

While there is a risk prices on some of those goods being imported from the US could rise, the more likely scenario is that consumers will turn to domestic alternatives, according to Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.

He says Carney's latest move has intentionally targeted goods where Canadians can "shift to domestic suppliers instead".

"Like hair care products, you really can just buy that domestically instead," he adds.

Saunders explains Carney's response aims to "minimise the impact on Canadian households as much as possible by picking very fungible goods".

The Budget Lab at Yale, which monitors the impact of US government policy on the economy, says it anticipates seeing marginal increases in furnishing and other household equipment for Americans largely due to tariffs on lumber and other materials.

There may not be a material impact on alcohol prices, but it's clear the trade war has had an impact on Canadians' choice of drink.

Many provinces in the country banned US alcohol sales last year in response to previous tariffs, with the American wine and spirits industry saying exports to the country dropped more than 70%.

Carney asked the provinces to restore US alcohol to the shelves during trade talks, but now that they have collapsed, it's likely the ban will return.

Saunders says there's been a big push to "buy Canadian" from politicians and it has been successful when it comes to the strong stuff.

"That's really had an impact on the American alcohol industry," he adds.

Saskatchewan and Alberta are ​the only provinces that still sell ​American alcohol, but the former has announced its own 50% charge on US imported booze, set to kick in on 8 September, when the wider Canadian tariffs do.

While tariffs can end up hitting consumers in the pocket, there are other impacts on households.

Import taxes can complicate trade for businesses that have cross-border supply. As well as the higher costs, the uncertainty created by the trade war could put off investment plans and stunt job creation.

Saunders suggests the biggest impact on households may not just be through prices, but job losses instead.

"If you're, let's say, a bespoke furniture producer in BC [British Columbia], you're now facing a 50% tariff on your exports to the US - that could really shut the business down. I think that would be more the direct impact on households as opposed to these retaliatory measures."

Canada's forest industry employs almost 200,000 people and has called on the government to boost domestic demand through federal housing programs to make greater use of Canadian wood, though it admits "no support package can replace reliable access to our largest export market".

When it comes to US, consumers are unlikely to see much of a difference in terms of the cost of living as result of this latest battle with Canada, but frictions to trade can have longer-term economic impacts.

Such tensions also feed into concerns over the free-trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form.

Despite the deal remaining operational, tariffs risk putting off talks in the near future, creating more uncertainty for cross-border trade.

John Iselin, associate director at the Budget Lab at Yale, estimates the cost will only be about $3 per American household on average, but when taking into account Trump's wider trade war with the rest of the world, and particularly China, the added costs rise to about $1,000 for the average family.

"It's hard to view this particular instance with Canada in isolation because we've had similar interactions with a range of other countries, all of which makes doing business harder. It's just another in a series of tariff shocks."

articles.title: Fresh avalanche & overflowing lake disrupt rescue operations in Nepal
articles.summary: South Asia News: Rescue teams on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border were repeatedly forced to reassess and retreat Friday as an unstable barrier lake overflowed into.
articles.body: Rescue teams on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border were repeatedly forced to reassess and retreat Friday as an unstable barrier lake overflowed into Bhote Koshi, sent a fresh surge downstream and briefly halted operations, only for another avalanche hours later to dump an estimated 50,000 cubic metres of ice debris towards the impounded water. Satellite images later showed an even more worrying development — a second, larger upstream lake was still growing and had no visible outlet. Officials said flood risk would remain until both lakes drained.The immediate scare began Friday morning when the debris-dammed lake near the Chhochen Khola-Purepu Tsangpo river system, upstream of the Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi corridor, began overflowing. Its volume had risen to more than 2.5 million cubic metres from an estimated 1.5-2 million cubic metres a day earlier.China ordered all rescue personnel and vehicles downstream to withdraw to designated safe areas amid fears that the debris barrier could fail and trigger another flood, landslide or avalanche. Nepal halted helicopter rescue operations in Rasuwa for around 90 minutes, while residents in vulnerable areas moved to higher ground.The fresh surge travelled downstream through Bhote Koshi towards Trishuli, prompting warnings to settlements along the river corridor. Nepal had initially received information that the barrier lake had “breached”, but later assessments did not confirm a catastrophic dam failure.Chinese embassy in Kathmandu said the lake remained at a high level and was overflowing. “The situation is currently at a critical stage for rescue and emergency response,” an embassy spokesperson said. Nepal planned to install cameras and sensors downstream while relying meanwhile on satellite imagery to track the lakes.Separately, Nepal closely monitored two glaciers next to the one that collapsed from Langtang Lirung on Wednesday after Chinese drone images appeared to show cracks in the ice, raising concern over slopes feeding the same Lhende river system. Hanging glaciers can be particularly hazardous because ice clings to steep slopes and can break away suddenly. Officials cautioned that the fissures could have existed for years and did not by themselves indicate an imminent collapse. “But given what has happened with the nearby glacier, we are trying to monitor this as much as possible,” an official from Nepal’s department of hydrology and meteorology told a climate news website.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The race to stop England running out of water
articles.summary: Who is to blame for the summer drought, and can England future-proof its water supplies?
articles.body:
One evening in early August, farmer Daniel Sizer's phone buzzed with a message.

It was from his local water board and it read: "River levels are low but have recovered enough to allow one night of irrigation tonight."

Like much of the lower half of England, Daniel's fourth-generation farm had seen barely any rain in nearly three months.

He shows us what is left of the peas and wheat crop at his 300-hectare site in Suffolk.

"There's no water in the river so half my crop is completely and utterly ruined."

With river levels falling so low that taking any more water out of them risked endangering wildlife, in July the Environment Agency (EA) temporarily stopped Daniel and thousands of other farmers from watering their crops from the river.

England has long been used to hosepipe bans over the summer.

But what Daniel has experienced points to something newer and more worrying. The kind of increasingly frequent heatwaves and greatly reduced rainfall that we have seen over successive summers, plus a projected increase in demand for water, have raised the prospect that England could at some point run out of water.

The result could be that by 2055 England will face a shortfall of five billion litres in public water supply a day, almost enough to fill Wembley Stadium four and a half times daily. A mixture of low rainfall, high temperatures and demand put pressure on water supply in England more so than elsewhere in the UK.

It is all a far cry from when, in 1818, John Keats wrote: "It is impossible to live in a country which is continually under hatches… Rain! Rain! Rain!"

But what is really to blame for England finding its water supply so under threat? And are there ways of securing its future?

Back in the 1980s, people in England and Denmark were using water at a similar rate. But no longer.

Residents in Denmark now consume 97 litres of water per person per day, according to Danva, the country's water and wastewater industry body. The daily consumption per person in England is 136.5 litres.

"We've actually doubled the amount of water we use per person, on average, in the last 50, 60 years," points out Nicci Russell, who runs Waterwise, a water efficiency campaign organisation.

She points to changing habits over generations - from a family having a shared bath once a week to having multiple showers a week, sometimes a day.

Households are responsible for nearly 60% of water use in England and Wales. If we had domestic water consumption patterns more like Denmark, Russell says, more than half the 2055 shortfall would be wiped out.

So how could water use in England come down to the levels seen in Denmark?

Russell says, even with projected population growth, if everyone in England knocked a minute off their shower time, for example, it would save nearly one billion litres of water a day by 2050.

But water companies have been running campaigns urging us to use less water, seemingly with limited success.

Will Willoughby, director of water supply at Wessex Water, acknowledges that the negative public perception of the water industry has limited the impact of the message, and the government may be better placed to deliver it.

"I think that would absolutely go a long way to… undoing some of the disdain towards the water companies and get people on board to help look after our water resources."

What really separates England and Denmark is price. As well as water meters being mandatory in Denmark, they also pay far more for their water than we do here.

Despite climbing water bills across the UK - and with them outrage aimed at water companies who stand accused of paying dividends to shareholders when they should have been investing in infrastructure - there is an argument to be made that consumers are actually not paying enough.

In Denmark, the average cost of water and wastewater is £9.45 per cubic metre, here it is significantly lower. Thames Water - one of the cheapest - charges £4.21 and Southern the most expensive at £7.06.

Daniel Johns, managing director of Water Resources East, an organisation working with farmers, water companies and local authorities, says water in England is "too cheap".

"People assume that it will always be readily available. And we need to wean ourselves off that kind of idea that water will always be there."

As it happens, price increases in Denmark were originally implemented for improved sewage treatment, the same reason people in England now face rising bills.

The behaviour change followed naturally as people became more careful with using the newly expensive utility, and it became embedded in the culture. School children have outings to waterworks to understand how precious the resource is, and households have embraced water-saving devices for shower heads and toilet cisterns.

This summer commentators have been discussing surge charging in England - higher rates for those using more water - but as prices are fixed in advance this is not possible under industry regulations.

Feargal Sharkey, former frontman of punk band The Undertones turned frontman of the water quality movement, summed up the feeling of campaigners towards efforts to raise prices and cut households consumption on Radio 4's Today programme earlier this month.

"All of this is nothing more than window dressing on the part of companies why they continue to abuse and exploit their customers."

Overconsumption of water is not just an issue for households. Businesses are estimated to use nearly a third of the water supply in England and Wales, with just under half of that coming from only 1% of companies.

And businesses have actually been receiving discounted charges from water companies that offer reduced rates the more water they use. Five of the nine water companies are now phasing this out over concerns it "might be sending the wrong signal on water efficiency", the industry regulator Ofwat has said.

And there is another question - are we doing enough to make sure businesses are using the right kind of water?

Potable water is water that is free of harmful bacteria and chemicals and is considered safe to drink and cook with. Non-potable water has not been treated to the same levels and is not safe for drinking but can be used in industrial settings and for irrigation.

"At the moment, we're using world-class drinking water to cool data centres, to irrigate our golf courses," Daniel Johns says.

He wants the regulator to look at removing access to drinking water for some businesses.

"We should simply ban data centres from using potable water supplies. We should require them to use closed-loop systems".

Despite recent well-publicised problems around burst water mains, water leakage has actually been cut by 43% since 1989 according to Ofwat, the water regulatory body for England and Wales.

However, more than 45 litres per person per day is still being lost from England's water network, nearly a fifth of all the water in the system.

And this is why following Denmark's lead by making meters mandatory could have an effect that goes beyond tying consumers' actual water usage to their bills.

When metered customers get higher than expected bills, that can be the clue water companies need to identify a leak and fix it. Without the meter, leaks are far harder to detect within pipes on private property.

Lightsonic is a company working with Affinity Water to speed up identification of leaks, and their secret weapon is fibre optic cables.

Internet cables often lie close to our water supply, and when water leaks it creates vibrations which interact with the cables and change the characteristics of the light travelling down the fibre optic, explains James Ramsay, chief technology officer at Lightsonic.

"We are just three months into our deployment and the technology has already helped locate over 100 leaks, which has saved the equivalent of two million litres of water every day."

Applied across the whole water network of England and Wales he boldly estimates it could reduce leakage "by as much as a billion litres a day".

England is already experiencing wetter winters, something climate models predict will continue. This prompts the question of whether we could just store more of this excess water for when we need it?

To do this, new reservoirs would be needed. But England has built no major new major reservoirs for more than 30 years.

The reason for the lack of new storage sites has been hotly debated between water companies and campaigners, the latter saying there has been a lack of investment from the privatised sector, the former arguing they were not given permission to spend the money by the regulators because of the impact on water bills.

The government's landmark independent Cunliffe review into the water sector in 2025 accepted that both arguments were true.

Now 10 reservoirs are planned in England by 2050. But even with financial and political backing, building new reservoirs is not straightforward.

"Building enough reservoirs to hold all that water requires good places, which means places where the land is sloping, where we can find a valley," explains Dr Ross Woods, associate professor of water and environmental engineering at the University of Bristol.

"I don't think that's realistic countrywide."

One of the sites found to be suitable for a mega-reservoir serving 15 million people is near Abingdon.

This picturesque Oxfordshire town on the banks of the River Thames, was until recently, perhaps most famed for its bun-throwing traditions, but it is now at the centre of a national debate.

Public opinion on the reservoir has been split - some have objected to using the site for water, fearing high environmental costs from the destruction of ancient woodlands.

The government has now designated it and one other reservoir as Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects, bypassing some local decision-making processes.

But these designations do not overcome the environmental hurdles.

Reservoirs, as water bodies, have to achieve "good" status for water quality under environmental law - meaning it must be free from pollution such as from agricultural runoff and invasive species - which just 14% of bodies currently in England have achieved. The Environment Agency told the Cunliffe Review that "the treatment costs of meeting 'good' may render the new reservoirs infeasible".

Even if these challenges are navigated, most of the reservoirs are not set for completion for at least a decade and once all are built they will only make up 7% of that 2055 shortfall.

We do have access to natural reservoirs - underground stores of water called aquifers.

This groundwater provides about one third of the public water supplies in England, and for some regions as much as 100%. They are vital sources of water supply to rivers, which are the first to struggle in summer droughts, and could be another solution to water shortages.

These underground stores can be recharged artificially during wet periods, providing a constant supply through drier summers, by encouraging excess rainfall to soak into soils rather than enter drainage networks as happens in heavily built-up urban areas.

These sustainable drainage systems, which include measures such as expanding grass areas and soakaways, are encouraged in new developments. However, this is predominantly where there is a risk of flooding not as a drought-prevention measure - and there is no legal requirement to have them.

When water supplies are no longer plentiful, tough choices have to be made.

As well as Daniel Sizer's Suffolk farm, the EA has now suspended or limited 1,327 farm licences for abstraction - taking water from rivers.

Paul Tomkins, the Deputy President of the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales, says the problem is there are legal frameworks in place to ensure there is enough water for nature and to protect the supply for households, but none for growing food.

"Farming is the poor brother of the triplets," says Paul.

How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar

How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con

After record heat, could the Atlantic make Britain's weather even more extreme?

With no rain and no river water, farms like Daniel's are facing insurmountable water shortages now - not in 2055.

"We can't afford to have another year like that. We're pretty much on the edge of of bankruptcy."

Woods says this will only be solved if society can agree how water should be used. "The limits that we're up against at the moment are environmental limits. It's not just how much water, it's how we use it as a society, and what values we put on the different uses of water. This is going to be one of the big challenges for water in the next 20 or 30 years".
